facts.claim: Subjective well-being of residents who commute by walking or cycling was significantly lower than that of those who commute by other transportation modes.
facts.quote: The subjective well-being of residents who commute by walking or cycling was significantly lower than that of those who commute by other transportation modes.

facts.claim: Longer commute times are more strongly negatively associated with the job satisfaction of women compared to men.

facts.claim: The longer the commute time, the lower the subjective well-being.
facts.quote: The regression results indicated that the longer the commute time, the lower the subjective well-being.

facts.claim: The absence of the commute, via working from home, is associated with increased job satisfaction and leisure time satisfaction.
facts.quote: The absence of the commute, via working from home, is associated with increased job satisfaction and leisure time satisfaction.

research.angle: While longer commutes are linked to lower subjective well-being, walking to work is associated with increased leisure time satisfaction and reduced strain.
research.verdict: The evidence shows that longer commutes generally correlate with lower well-being and job satisfaction, but the impact varies significantly by transport mode and gender.
research.caveat: The findings are largely based on observational studies and systematic reviews, meaning they show associations rather than proving that commuting causes lower well-being.
